## Learning goals

You will build a model for daily ozone in New York (May–September 1973) step by step: from a linear model, through a choice of response scale and family, to an additive model with smooth terms, an interaction surface and a short written interpretation. By the end you should be able to:

- diagnose from residual plots when a linear predictor misses non-linear effects;
- fit GAMs with `mgcv::gam()` using REML, and read edf, approximate tests and partial-effect plots;
- check a GAM with `gam.check()` (basis dimension $k$) and `concurvity()`;
- compare an additive model with a tensor-product interaction `te(Temp, Wind)` by AIC;
- turn a GAM into predictions with honest uncertainty and explain them in plain words.

Work in pairs. The lab takes 60–75 minutes. Answer the questions in `tutorial.Rmd` as you go; the `.txt` it produces is your submission.

## Setup

```{r}
library(mgcv)      # gam(), gam.check(), concurvity(), vis.gam()
library(gratia)    # draw(), appraise()
aq_all <- read.csv("data/airquality.csv")
dim(aq_all)
colSums(is.na(aq_all))
```

The data set has 153 days. `Ozone` (ppb, mean between 13:00 and 15:00) is missing on 37 days and `Solar.R` (solar radiation, Langleys) on 7. `Wind` is average wind speed (mph) and `Temp` the daily maximum temperature (°F). We model ozone from the three meteorological variables, so we keep the complete cases. We also add the day of the season, which we need later to check the residuals in time order.

```{r}
aq_all$day <- seq_len(nrow(aq_all))          # 1 = 1 May 1973
aq <- na.omit(aq_all)
nrow(aq)
```

**Your turn.** How many days are left? Which variable causes most of the loss? Could dropping these days bias the analysis? (Think about why ozone might be missing.)

## A linear model and its residuals

Start with the model you would have fitted in Session 6:

$$\text{Ozone}_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{Solar.R}_i+\beta_2\,\text{Wind}_i+\beta_3\,\text{Temp}_i+\varepsilon_i .$$

```{r}
lm_raw <- lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R + Wind + Temp, data = aq)
summary(lm_raw)$coefficients
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fitted(lm_raw), resid(lm_raw), xlab = "Fitted", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
lines(lowess(fitted(lm_raw), resid(lm_raw)), col = "red", lwd = 2)
plot(aq$Temp, resid(lm_raw), xlab = "Temp", ylab = "Residual")
lines(lowess(aq$Temp, resid(lm_raw)), col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

Two problems show up: the residuals curve (U shape against the fitted values), and their spread grows with the fitted value. A log transformation addresses the second; it does not, by itself, address the first.

```{r}
lm_log <- lm(log(Ozone) ~ Solar.R + Wind + Temp, data = aq)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
for (v in c("Solar.R", "Wind", "Temp")) {
  plot(aq[[v]], resid(lm_log), xlab = v, ylab = "Residual (log scale)")
  lines(lowess(aq[[v]], resid(lm_log)), col = "red", lwd = 2)
  abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
}
```

**Your turn.** Describe in one sentence each the pattern of the residuals against `Solar.R` and against `Wind`. Which covariate looks most clearly non-linear?

## Choosing the response scale and the family

A positive, right-skewed response can be handled in two ways:

1. transform it: a Gaussian model for $\log y$, so $e^{\hat\eta}$ estimates the **median** ozone;
2. keep it and choose a family: a Gamma model with log link, $\log \mathrm{E}(y)=\eta$, $\mathrm{Var}(y)=\phi\mu^2$, so $e^{\hat\eta}$ estimates the **mean**.

We fit both, with the same smooth terms (next section explains `s()`):

```{r}
m_log   <- gam(log(Ozone) ~ s(Solar.R) + s(Wind) + s(Temp),
               data = aq, method = "REML")
m_gamma <- gam(Ozone ~ s(Solar.R) + s(Wind) + s(Temp),
               family = Gamma(link = "log"), data = aq, method = "REML")
m_ident <- gam(Ozone ~ s(Solar.R) + s(Wind) + s(Temp),
               data = aq, method = "REML")
```

`AIC(m_log)` is computed from the density of $\log y$, the other two from the density of $y$. Since $f_Y(y)=f_{\log Y}(\log y)/y$, we have $\text{AIC}_Y=\text{AIC}_{\log Y}+2\sum_i\log y_i$:

```{r}
c(gaussian_identity = AIC(m_ident),
  gaussian_log_y    = AIC(m_log) + 2 * sum(log(aq$Ozone)),
  gamma_log_link    = AIC(m_gamma))
```

**Your turn.** Which model has the lowest AIC on the Ozone scale? Why would comparing `AIC(m_log)` with `AIC(m_gamma)` directly be meaningless? In the rest of the lab we use the Gaussian model for $\log(\text{Ozone})$ because its residuals are easy to inspect; everything works the same with the Gamma family.

## An additive model with REML

The additive model replaces each straight line by a smooth function:

$$\log(\text{Ozone}_i)=\beta_0+f_1(\text{Solar.R}_i)+f_2(\text{Wind}_i)+f_3(\text{Temp}_i)+\varepsilon_i ,\qquad \textstyle\sum_i f_j(x_{ij})=0 .$$

Each `s()` is a thin-plate regression spline with $k=10$ basis functions and a penalty $\lambda_j\int f_j''(x)^2dx$. We choose the smoothing parameters by REML. **The default of `gam()` is `method = "GCV.Cp"`**, which tends to undersmooth; compare:

```{r}
summary(m_log)
m_gcv <- gam(log(Ozone) ~ s(Solar.R) + s(Wind) + s(Temp), data = aq)
round(cbind(REML = summary(m_log)$edf, GCV = summary(m_gcv)$edf), 2)
AIC(lm_log, m_log)
```

The intercept equals the mean of $\log(\text{Ozone})$ because every smooth is centred. Each edf tells you how many degrees of freedom the smooth uses: 1 is a straight line.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.5
draw(m_log, residuals = TRUE)
```

**Your turn.** (a) Which smooth has the largest edf with REML? (b) Which smooth changes most with GCV, and in which direction? (c) Describe the shape of the Wind effect, including where the band is widest and why.

## Checking the fit: `gam.check()` and the basis dimension

`gam.check()` prints convergence information, four residual plots, and a test of whether $k$ is large enough. The k-index compares differences between residuals that are neighbours in a covariate with the overall residual variance; values well below 1, with edf close to $k'=k-1$, suggest increasing $k$. The $p$-values come from permutations, so set a seed.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
set.seed(1)
gam.check(m_log)
```

`s(Wind)` has a k-index of about 0.86. Does a larger basis help?

```{r}
m_k20 <- gam(log(Ozone) ~ s(Solar.R) + s(Wind, k = 20) + s(Temp),
             data = aq, method = "REML")
set.seed(1)
k.check(m_k20)
```

**Your turn.** What happened to the edf and the k-index of `s(Wind)` when $k$ went from 10 to 20? What does that tell you about the cause of the low k-index? Keep that question in mind for Section 7.

## Concurvity

Temperature and wind are related (hot days tend to be calm). When one smooth can be approximated by the others, the model cannot tell well which covariate an effect belongs to: this is *concurvity*, the non-linear analogue of collinearity.

```{r}
cor(aq[, c("Solar.R", "Wind", "Temp")])
round(concurvity(m_log, full = TRUE), 3)
round(concurvity(m_log, full = FALSE)$estimate, 3)
```

Each entry is between 0 (no concurvity) and 1 (the term is fully explained by the others). A common rule of thumb is to worry above about 0.8.

**Your turn.** Which smooth has the highest `worst` concurvity? Is concurvity a problem here? What would change in the partial-effect plots if it were close to 1?

## An interaction: `te(Temp, Wind)`

Ozone builds up on days that are both hot and calm. An additive model forces the effect of temperature to be the same at every wind speed. A tensor-product smooth `te(Temp, Wind)` lets the surface bend freely, with one smoothing parameter per direction, so it does not depend on the units of the two covariates. The ANOVA version `s(Wind) + s(Temp) + ti(Temp, Wind)` keeps the main effects and adds a pure interaction term.

```{r}
m_te <- gam(log(Ozone) ~ s(Solar.R) + te(Temp, Wind), data = aq, method = "REML")
m_ti <- gam(log(Ozone) ~ s(Solar.R) + s(Wind) + s(Temp) + ti(Temp, Wind),
            data = aq, method = "REML")
summary(m_te)$s.table
summary(m_ti)$s.table
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
vis.gam(m_te, view = c("Temp", "Wind"), plot.type = "contour",
        too.far = 0.1, main = "te(Temp, Wind): linear predictor")
points(aq$Temp, aq$Wind, pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
```

`too.far = 0.1` blanks the surface where there are no data nearby. Always use it for two-dimensional smooths.

**Your turn.** (a) Where in the (Temp, Wind) plane is ozone highest? (b) Re-run `k.check(m_ti)` (after `set.seed(1)`): what happened to the k-index of `s(Wind)`? (c) The `ti` term is significant, but `s(Wind)` is not. Does that mean wind does not matter?

## Model comparison by AIC

All the models below have the same response, $\log(\text{Ozone})$, and the same 111 days, so their AICs are comparable. `mgcv`'s AIC uses effective degrees of freedom corrected for the uncertainty in the smoothing parameters.

```{r}
AIC(lm_log, m_log, m_te, m_ti)
```

For a test of the interaction, compare nested models fitted by ML (REML scores are not comparable between models with different unpenalized parts). The test is approximate.

```{r}
m_add_ml <- gam(log(Ozone) ~ s(Solar.R) + s(Wind) + s(Temp), data = aq, method = "ML")
m_ti_ml  <- gam(log(Ozone) ~ s(Solar.R) + s(Wind) + s(Temp) + ti(Temp, Wind),
                data = aq, method = "ML")
anova(m_add_ml, m_ti_ml, test = "F")
```

Finally, check the residuals of the chosen model in time order: consecutive days could be correlated.

```{r}
r <- residuals(m_ti)
ok <- diff(aq$day) == 1
c(lag1 = cor(r[-length(r)][ok], r[-1][ok]), pairs = sum(ok))
plot(aq$day, r, xlab = "day of season", ylab = "residual"); abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
lines(lowess(aq$day, r), col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

**Your turn.** Which model do you choose and why (two reasons)? Is there evidence of serial correlation that would require a correlation structure (Session 27)?

## Predictions and partial effects you can explain

Partial effects are centred and on the link scale. To communicate a model, translate it into predictions on the scale of the data, with intervals built on the link scale and then transformed.

```{r}
nd <- expand.grid(Temp = c(70, 80, 90), Wind = c(5, 10, 15),
                  Solar.R = median(aq$Solar.R))
pr <- predict(m_ti, nd, se.fit = TRUE)
nd$median_ozone <- exp(pr$fit)
nd$lower <- exp(pr$fit - 1.96 * pr$se.fit)
nd$upper <- exp(pr$fit + 1.96 * pr$se.fit)
round(nd, 1)
```

A contrast between two predictions has its own standard error. Use the linear-predictor matrix:

```{r}
X <- predict(m_ti, data.frame(Temp = c(70, 90), Wind = 10, Solar.R = 207),
             type = "lpmatrix")
d <- X[2, ] - X[1, ]
est <- sum(d * coef(m_ti))
se  <- sqrt(drop(t(d) %*% vcov(m_ti) %*% d))
exp(c(ratio = est, lower = est - 1.96 * se, upper = est + 1.96 * se))
```

**Your turn.** Write the result of the contrast as a sentence a city official would understand. Then predict the median ozone for a day with Temp $=85$ °F, Wind $=7$ mph and Solar.R $=250$, with a 95% interval.
